messages.subject_clean: Save .Rdata file that is ~1gb in size
messages.body_plain:

If I try to save the list object as a .Rdata file using save.image(), R crashes.

Is there any way to maybe compress the the list object or any other workaround for this?

Thanks
Ross

You can get a complete list of available window functions with

help(ftwindow)

best,
jesse

messages.subject: Problem with writeWave after using ffilter: file contains no sound
messages.subject_clean: Problem with writeWave after using ffilter: file contains no sound
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,
The problem I am having can be reproduced as follows

library(wave)
data(tico)
f<-ffilter(tico, from = 2.78-0.5, to = 2.78+0.5, output="Wave") # the from and to numbers aren't really important here
writeWave(f,"sample.wav")
Warning message:
In writeWave(f, "sample.wav") :
  channels' data will be rounded to integers for writing the wave file

When I try to play the file I get, it plays, but there is no sound.  What is going on here, and how can I fix it?

Cheers!

messages.subject: Release of seewave 1.7.3
messages.body_plain:
Dear seewave users,

A new version of seewave (1.7.3) is on CRAN now.

New features:

o acoustat(): a new function to obtain statistics on the time and
frequency contours of the short-term Fourier transform, following the
principles described by Fristrup and Watkins (1992). Checked by K. Fristrup.

o NDSI(): a new function to obtain a Symbolic Aggregate approXimation of
a numeric vector as described in Lin et al. (2003). Checked by E. Kasten.

o SAX(): a new function to compute the Normalized Difference Soundscape
Index as described in Kasten et al. (2003). Checked by E. Kasten.

o soundscapespec(): a new function to compute a frequency spectrum
according to soundscape description as described in Kasten et al.
(2012). Checked by E. Kasten.

o TKEO(): a new function to compute the Teager-Kaiser Energy Operator.

o zcr(): a new function to compute the zero-crossing rate.

Thanks very much to Eric Kasten, Stuart Gage and Kurt Fristrup for their
help!

Enjoy,

Jerome

messages.subject: acoustat function
messages.body_plain:
Bonjour Jerôme,
Meilleurs voeux pour la nouvelle année.

I have been looking at the new acoustat routine in v1.7.3 (along with the papers on it). A couple of observations, please correct me if I'm wrong:

As far as I can see, calculating the "aggregate power spectrum" via the DFT only has an advantage if one uses it for low (and/or high) frequency noise elimination. This could be done easily, with an added user-selected parameter in the command line and only a minor addition to the coding (in the f.cont lines?).
To do it, instead of summing the power at every frequency band in a DFT, one only sums the powers above a minumum frequency and then noise below that frequency is eliminated from the spectrum. Of course it only works for sounds that are not "buried" in the noise (vocalisations in the 0-2kHz range for example) but then the user could set the minimum frequency to 0. High frequency noise could also be eliminated this way but I've never met it as a problem. (Fristrup & Watkins remove noise before the calculation but maybe whale vocalisations are buried in aquatic noise, Cortopassi also insists on prior noise-removal but most song bird vocalisations are above 2kHz and the above method seems simpler and less error-prone).

Otherwise, without this noise reduction, using DFTs for the calculation seems excessive. With DFT windows of n samples, the "aggregate power spectrum" merely corresponds to the squared sum, over n samples, of the sound amplitudes in each (overlapping) window of the time domain spectrum, i.e. a smoothed and squared time domain spectrum. This can be calculated much more simply and rapidly without calculating the DFTs and without the corresponding (small) errors introduced.

For those tempted to try it,  the aggregate power spectrum, with noise elimination,  should be useful for automatic detection of sound element lengths and intervals BUT the squaring causes a problem because it magnifies amplitude fluctuations within an element. Using a log (dB) scale may overcome this.

All the best,
Krzysz
